en: The *Sarvavajrodaya*: A Ritual Manual for the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, composed by Ānandagarbha.
Edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai (Research Group on Esoteric Buddhist Scriptures).
%%% In *Taishō University Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Kiyō* 8 (1986),
pp. 253(28)–225(56) % From Ryūgen Tanemura

(1) Thereafter, having empowered oneself in the four places by means of Vajradhātvīśvarī and having formed the Bodhyagrī mudrā, one should urge the Vajrasattva residing in the heart, saying "Vajrasattva.

(2) Then, [rays] emerging from the hearts of all the Tathāgatas become moon-maṇḍalas and, having gone forth, cause all sentient beings throughout all world-systems to realize selflessness; then, having produced one-pointedness of mind in the form of moon-maṇḍalas, one should contemplate that they return and remain as moon-maṇḍalas alone in the places of all the deities.

(3) Then, rays of wisdom emanating from them enter the vajra within one’s own heart; having merged with it through the empowerment of all the Tathāgatas, they become a great five-pronged vajra-form whose magnitude is equal to the entire expanse of space. Once again, returning to the exact size of the vajra previously in the heart, they emerge from it and one should contemplate them as being held in one’s own hand.

Furthermore, from that, vajra-shaped rays of light of many colors and many forms issue forth and pervade the entire realm of space. From those, again, in the form of Vajrasattva and others, they pervade the entire realm of sentient beings. From those, again, in the form of Vajrasattva and others, they engage the entire realm of sentient beings in the realization of the primordial wisdom of the equality of all Tathāgatas and so forth.

Then, through the yoga of reabsorption, becoming the body of a single being, they enter the vajra located at one's own heart; while remaining there, one should contemplate [the deity] uttering an inspired utterance (*udāna*).
"Aha! I am Samantabhadra, the firm being among the self-arisen ones; because of my firmness, though bodiless, I have attained the state of the body of a being.
Thus [he said].

Then, one should visualize [the disciple] descending from the heart, standing before Akṣobhya, and seeking his command. Then, having consecrated him for the sovereignty over the wheel of the family of all Tathāgatas by means of the crown and ribbon consecration of the five Buddhas, one should give the Primordial Vajra—which brings about the realization of the supreme morality and so forth, up to the perfect awakening of the knowledge of the equality of all Tathāgatas, marked with the Primordial Vajra and accompanied by a bell—to Samantabhadra for the sake of accomplishing the entire realm of sentient beings without exception.
(5) Then one should bestow the name-consecration and so forth; following that, one should utter an exclamation with the pride of being Vajrapāṇi.
This is that unsurpassed Vajra of Accomplishment of all Buddhas;
I have placed it in my hand—the Vajra established within the Vajra. (1)
Thus it is said.
(6) Thus, while reciting the exclamation (*udāna*) concerning the arising, expansion, withdrawal, abiding, and firming [of the mandala], and its residence within the vajra at the heart of Vairocana,
one should visualize it extending as far as the *vajramuṣṭi*.
These are the exclamations of Vajrarāja and the others.
Aho! I am indeed the King of the Unfailing, the Vajra-born Hook, by which all the Buddhas who pervade everything are drawn forth for the sake of accomplishment. (1)
This is that unsurpassed vajra-wisdom of all Buddhas;
it is the supreme means of summoning for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all Buddhas. (2) Thus it is said.

"Aha! My own nature is pure; such is the spontaneous passion of the Self-Arisen Ones, that for the sake of purification, they indeed discipline those who are detached through passion. (3) Thus it is said.
This is that unclouded knowledge of passion belonging to all the Buddhas;
for by destroying dispassion through passion, they bestow all happiness. (4) Thus it is said.
"Aho! Indeed, I am the one who utters the word of praise; I am all, the best among the all-knowing.

For this is the divine Vajra that brings about the word of praise for those who have abandoned conceptual construction, which causes the satisfaction of all and increases supreme joy. (6) Thus it is said.
"Aho! I am indeed the self-consecrated, the unsurpassed Vajraratna, for even the Victors, though free from attachment, are remembered as the lords of the three realms. (7)
"This is that consecration of all the Buddhas in all realms; I have placed the jewel in my hand, and the jewel has been applied to the jewel. (8) Thus it is said.
Oh, how inconceivable is my splendor, which illuminates all realms and impels even the pure Buddhas, the Protectors! (9)
This is that which destroys the darkness of ignorance for all Buddhas, possessing a radiance exceeding even the suns as numerous as atoms of dust. (10)
"Aho! I am indeed the peerless banner named Sarvārthasiddhi (Accomplisher of All Aims), for it fulfills all hopes and completely accomplishes every purpose. (11) Thus.
This is that method of the perfection of generosity called the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Banner," which fulfills all the aspirations of all Buddhas.
Oh, what a great laugh! How truly marvelous it is that those who are always perfectly concentrated apply themselves for the sake of the Buddhas, the most eminent of all beings. (13)
This is that knowledge of all the Buddhas which demonstrates the arising of wonders, which produces great joy, and which is unknown to other teachers. (14) Thus it is said.
Oh, how wonderful! I am the ultimate reality, the primordial purity of the self-arisen ones; for even among those who possess the nature of a raft, such purification is found. 15.
This is that realization of the reality of passion belonging to all Buddhas; "I" and "mine" are placed in the hand, the Dharma established within the Dharma. // 16 //
Oh, how I am mindful of the Mañjughoṣa of all the Buddhas, since through formless wisdom the state of being "Voice" (Ghoṣa) is perceived! 17.
This is that method of the perfection of wisdom of all Buddhas;
it is the supreme destroyer of all enemies and the remover of all sins. // 18 //

"Aho! This wheel is made of diamond; I am the foremost among those possessing the diamond-like Dharma, since by the mere arising of the thought [of awakening], the Wheel of Dharma is set in motion. (19)
This is that purification of all phenomena for all Buddhas;
it is known as the irreversible wheel, the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa). // 20 //
"Aho! I have now remembered the secret intentional language (*saṃdhābhāṣa*) of the Self-Existent Ones, by which they teach the True Dharma, free from the proliferation of speech. (21)
This is that vajra-recitation of all Buddhas, which immediately brings about the swift accomplishment of the mantras of all Tathāgatas. (22) Thus it is said.
Ah! Truly, the activity of the Buddhas is unfailing; I am manifold, for I set in motion the vajra-activity for the sake of the effortless purpose of the Buddhas. (23)
This is that supreme [mantra] which performs all activities for all Buddhas; I have placed it in my hand, and the universe has been employed within the universe. 24.
Oh, how marvelous! This armor consisting of vigor is most firm for those of steadfast mind;
because of its firmness, it is supreme in producing a vajra-body for those who are bodiless. 25.
This is that supreme armor of loving-kindness belonging to all Buddhas;
it is proclaimed as the great friend, a mighty protection of firm vigor. (26)
Oh, what a great expedient of the Buddhas, whose very nature is compassion! That for the sake of sentient beings, they who are peaceful even assume a fierce form. (27)
This is that [weapon] of all the Buddhas, the supreme subduer of all the wicked;
it is the sharp vajra-fang weapon, the skillful means of those whose nature is compassion. (28)
Oh, how firm indeed is the bond of the Samaya for those of steadfast soul, since it is a fetter even for the liberated, for the sake of accomplishing all their hopes! 29.
This is that very binding of the mudrās of all the Buddhas, most firmly established; it is the samaya for the purification of all Buddhas, which is difficult to transgress. Thus [it is said]. (30)
(7) Then, with the ego-identification of Akṣobhya, one should produce Sattvavajrī; with the ego-identification of Ratnasaṃbhava, Ratnavajrī;
and with the ego-identification of Amitābha, Dharmavajrī.
With the ego-identification of Amoghasiddhi, one [visualizes] Karmavajrī;
these are their respective udānas.
Aho! Indeed, among all Buddhas, I am the firm *sattvavajra*; because of that firmness, though I was once bodiless, I have attained the state of a vajra-body. (1)
Aho! Indeed, I am remembered as the Jewel-Vajra of all Buddhas, for I am the firm method of empowerment for all mudrās. (2)
Aho! I am indeed the pure Dharma-vajra of all Buddhas;
for through the purity of intrinsic nature, even passion is truly stainless. (3)
"Aho! Indeed, I am the manifold Vajra of Action of all the Buddhas, since, being one, I perform virtuous deeds for the entire realm of sentient beings. (4) Thus it is said.
(8) Furthermore, by means of the ego-identity of Vairocana, there is the quartet beginning with Lāsyā; their utterances are as follows:
"Aha! There is indeed no other worship equal to mine for the Self-Existent Ones."
Through the worship of sensual pleasures and delights, all forms of worship proceed. // 1 //
Oh, how truly incomparable is this so-called "offering of jewels," since those who have been fully honored rule over the supreme sovereignty of the three realms! // 2 //
Oh, how wonderful! I am an offering consisting of song for the All-Seeing Ones, since they are pleased by such offerings even though they are like echoes. (3)
Oh, how truly sublime is my worship! For among all those who perform acts of worship, it is this which constitutes the worship of the Buddhas through the ritual of Vajra-dance. (4)
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, by means of the ego-identification with Akṣobhya and the others, there are the four goddesses Vajradhūpā and so forth. Their utterances are as follows:
"Aho! Indeed, I am the Great Worship, auspicious and full of refreshment."
For by means of the yoga of entering into sentient beings, awakening is indeed swiftly attained. // 1 //
Ah, indeed, this flower-worship is the maker of all ornaments, since by worshipping the jewel-nature of the Tathāgata, it is swiftly attained. // 2 //
Oh, how truly sublime is this auspicious lamp-offering, by which one may swiftly attain the vision of all Buddhas, possessed of light! (3)
Oh, how wonderful! This divine worship consisting of fragrance is truly enchanting, for it indeed bestows the scent of the Tathāgata upon the entire body. (4)
Thus it is said.
(10) Therefore, through the ego-identity of Vairocana, there is the quartet beginning with the Vajra Hook; this is their inspired utterance (*udāna*):
"Aho! Indeed, I am the firm one who performs the summoning of all Buddhas."
For all those whom I have summoned indeed worship the entire maṇḍala. // 1 //
Aho! I am indeed the firm Vajra-noose of all the Buddhas, since even those who have already entered everywhere are made to enter by me once again. // 2 //
Oh, how firm indeed is my vajra-bond of all the Buddhas, since for those who are liberated from all fetters, bondage is desired for the sake of sentient beings! // 3 //
Aho! For I am firm in the vajra-entrance of all the Buddhas, such that having become lords of all, they indeed even become servants. 4.
Thus it is said.
By this much, it is called the samādhi known as Maṇḍalarājāgra.
(11) Then, having visualized oneself as inseparable from Vairocana, one should perform the assembly (*samāja*).
Then, toward all those Tathāgatas who have entered that assembly, together with their circles of Bodhisattva retinues:
*Oṃ, I pay homage at the feet of all the Tathāgatas.*
Having spoken thus:
"Oh, how great is the honor shown to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, that the Tathāgata shines in the midst of the wheel of the Tathāgatas! (1)
While they are uttering this inspired utterance (*udāna*), one should contemplate:
then, having entered the heart of Vairocana and emerged, becoming one with Sattvavajra and the others, they once again utter this inspired utterance:
"O, how great is the sublime generosity of all the Buddhas, born of no beginning!"
Indeed, those who have attained oneness through the sequential enumeration of the Arvāṇus are the Buddhas. // 1 //
Thus it is said.

(13) Then, the yogin, abiding in the state of Śrī Vajrasattva, having received the garland initiation and so forth from all the Tathāgatas, and having drawn them in, caused them to enter, bound them, and brought them under control by means of the vajra-hook and other implements, he establishes Vairocana and the others as sealed with the *caru*-mudrā; [this is] for the singular gathering of all Buddhas, for the sealing of all families,
and for the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
For the summoning of all Tathāgatas;
for the act of enchantment; for the act of pleasing.
In the consecration;
in the illumination by light;
and in the application to the perfection of giving.
In establishing the wonder of the smile,
in accomplishing the samādhi of perfect purity,
and in severing the afflictions and secondary afflictions.
In entering the great maṇḍala;
in being established in the state of non-proliferated reality (niṣprapañca-dharmatā);
and in worshipping all Tathāgatas through worship that is exhaustive and without remainder.
In guarding against longing for other vehicles and protecting against the afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and so forth;
in providing all-encompassing protection and preservation;
and in the accomplishment of all Buddhas through the fist-seal of suchness that binds body, speech, and mind into one.
In the accomplishment of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, wisdom, meditative concentration, aspiration, and skillful means;
in drawing all sentient beings toward the great city of liberation by means of the hook of the awakening mind;
and in entering [the path] through the practice of the ten perfections.
One should apply oneself to shattering the mind that desires other vehicles,
to the penetration of natural luminosity and non-arising,
and to the protection of the city of the True Dharma.
Thus ends the meditative absorption called "The Foremost King of Ritual Actions."
(14) Then, having sprinkled all the components of the offering with scented water consecrated by the Vajrayakṣa mantra,
and having consecrated them with the Vajrānala mudrā, [recite]:
*vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*.
Thus, with the flower mudrā, [offer] flowers:
Oṃ vajragandhe.
Thus, with the fragrance mudrā, [offer] fragrance.
Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ.
Thus, with the incense mudrā, one offers incense:
"A" is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the very beginning.
Thus, with the sword mudrā, [offer] the bali.
With the vajra-binding [mudrā], the gesture of drawing [the sword] from the scabbard is the sword mudrā;
*hūṃ vajrāloke*.
Thus, with the lamp mudrā, [offer] the lamp:
Oṃ Vajrasattva Hūṃ.

Thus, having placed sesame seeds, barley, kuśa grass, parched grain, black fragrant flowers, sandalwood, and water into a conch vessel or similar container, one should recite [the mantra] three times with the *argha* mudrā characterized by the open-vajra palms; then, having recited it seven or twenty-one times, one should set it aside.
(15) Then, having opened the door and bound the Great Mudrā of the glorious Vajrasattva, [one recites]:
*oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ*.
Having thus recited [the mantra],
with the two arms in the vajra-bind and by releasing the vajra-claps,
one who is the self of the yoga of Śrī Vajrasattva should assemble all the Buddhas. (1)
By clapping with the left hand in the *chaṭaka* rhythm, one achieves perfection; the clap with the right hand is likewise declared, as are both combined in the *saṃnipāta* rhythm. (2)
Thus ends the description of the mudrās of the assembly.
Oṃ vajrasamāja jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ.

Thus ends the Heart of the Samāja Mudrā. At the mere command of this [mantra], all the Buddhas, together with their assemblies and circles of retinues, arrive; what need is there to mention others? (3)
Then, quickly practicing the great mudrā of Vajrasattva,
one should recite the supreme eight-hundred-name mantra once.
"Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva," and so forth.
(16) Then, having performed the rites at all the gates with the hook and other [implements], one should establish the pledges by means of the great supreme action mudrās. // 1 //
Likewise, one should accomplish the Great Beings by means of the supreme samaya-mudrās, such as Sattvavajrī and the others, and should employ JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ. // 2 //
(17) This is what is meant:
having performed the expulsion of obstacles and the protective rites with Vajrayakṣa,
one should secure the doors with Vajramuṣṭi.
Having offered the *argha* with Vajrasattva and having bound the *samaya-mudrās* such as Vajradhātu and so forth,
one should cause all visible objects to appear by reciting "Vajradhātu dṛśya" and so on,
[and then say]: "Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ, you are the *samaya*."
You are the commitment; I am [the commitment].
Having recited three times the heart-mantras of Śrī Vairocana and the others from one's own heart,
and having consecrated the Buddhas and others with the Dharma-mudrās, Karma-mudrās, Mahāmudrās, and various other mudrās of consecration, and having offered the water of honor (*argha*),
[one should recite]: (18) *oṃ sarvatathāgatapuṣpapūjāmeghasamudraspharaṇasamaye hūṃ*.
Thus with flowers:
Oṃ, at the time of the pervasive ocean-clouds of offerings of fragrance of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ!
Thus with the scents:
Oṃ, at the time of the pervasive ocean-like cloud of incense offerings of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ!
Thus with incenses;
with "Oṃ, the letter A is the mouth of all phenomena," and so forth, with the offering of the bali;
"Oṃ, at the time of the pervasive ocean-like cloud of lamps as an offering to all Tathāgatas, hūṃ."
Thus, having worshipped with lamps and with the eightfold worship beginning with *lāsya*, [one recites]:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatasarvātmaniryātanapūjāspharaṇakarmavajrī āḥ*.
Oṃ! O foremost of those whose activity is the radiation of the worship that consists of the offering of one's entire self to all Tathāgatas! Jaḥ!
Oṃ, to the arrow of activity that radiates the offering of the loving attachment that offers up one's entire self to all Tathāgatas, hūṃ hoḥ!
Oṃ! To the satisfaction of the activity that radiates the offering of "Well Done! through the self-surrender of all Tathāgatas as one's own essence: Āḥ!
Oṃ, homage to the jewels of the empowerment of the bodies of all the Tathāgatas; Vajramaṇi, Oṃ!
Oṃ, homage to all the Tathāgata-suns! O Vajratejinī, blaze forth! Hrīḥ!
Oṃ, homage to those who are like wish-fulfilling jewels at the tips of the banners of all Tathāgatas, fulfilling their aspirations; O Vajradhvajāgra, Trāṃ!
Oṃ, homage to those who produce great joy and gladness for all Tathāgatas; O Vajrahāsa, Haḥ!
Oṃ! With the samādhis of the equality of the vajra-dharma of all Tathāgatas, I praise you, O Great Foremost of Dharmas, Hrīḥ!
Oṃ, I praise you, O Mahāghoṣānugā, through the emanations of the Prajñāpāramitā of all the Tathāgatas; dhaṃ!
Oṃ! I praise you with all the methods of the sūtras, beginning with the transformation of the syllables of the wheel of all Tathāgatas; in all maṇḍalas, hūṃ!
Oṃ, with the songs of the assemblies of Buddhas through the intentional language of all Tathāgatas, I praise you, O Vajravācī; vaṃ!
Oṃ! O you who perform the rite of worship by radiating clouds of incense from all the Tathāgatas! Kara kara!
Oṃ, for the ritual action of the pervasive emanation of the blossoming flowers of all Tathāgatas, kiri kiri!
Oṃ, perform the activity of worship by radiating the blazing light of all the Tathāgatas; *kara kara*.
Oṃ, perform, perform the rite of worship that radiates oceans of fragrance from all the Tathāgatas!
Thus, one should perform worship with these vidyās, which correspond to the sixteen sattvas and are joined with the karmamudrās.
In this regard, these mudrās are as follows: Having formed the vajra-bind in the body and split it into two with both fists,
one stands holding the goad with both hands while displaying pride and loftiness.
And through the application of vocal articulation, the sounds of approval (sādhukāra) reside within the heart. // 1 //
In the consecration, however, there is the display of the double-vajra at the heart;
and likewise, the staff-like arm situated on the left is turned toward the mouth. // 2 //
Blossoming to the right and left, she brandishes a sword in her heart and left hands;
whirled like a circle of fire, she issues from the two mouths of a vajra. // 3 //
With cheeks free from the whirling of the vajra-dance, she is situated upon the uṣṇīṣa;
she possesses armor, has the tips of her fangs on the little fingers, and is pressed by two fists. // 4 //
Thus it is said.

Then, having performed four prostrations and being established in the great mudrā of Śrī Vajrasattva, one should meditate upon oneself as the vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas with this [mantra]:
Oṃ vajrātmako ’ham.
Thus it is said.
Then: "Inherently pure;
Oṃ, I am inherently pure."
Thus [it is said].
And through the equality of selflessness, one possesses the intrinsic nature of all deities, such as Vairocana and others:
Oṃ, I am equal to all.
Thus it is said.

(22) Then, uttering the hundred-syllable mantra of Śrī Vajrasattva with the vajra-voice, one should mentally cultivate the thought, "I am indeed all. One should maintain the conviction that the sound of the mantra resounds from the mouths of all the deities. In this way, they become recited by everyone. One should meditate until weariness arises.

When weariness occurs, one should again offer the hymn of one hundred and eight names, present the *argha* offering, perform worship, and make the four prostrations; then, one should release the mudrās at the very places from which they were generated—this is the release of the Sattvavajrī and other mudrās.
Vajrasattva muḥ.
Thus it is said.
(23) The rule regarding the locations of Śrī Vajrasattva and the others has been stated.

The very place of Akṣobhya and the others— Vajrasattva, Vajraratna, Vajradharma, and Vajrakarma— is the place of Vairocana’s uṣṇīṣa. Then, one should perform the consecration of all mudrās by means of the Vajraratna-samaya-mudrā, which has arisen from the heart and is situated at the place of one's own consecration.
Oṃ, consecrate with the vajra-jewel!
Thus it is said.
Thereafter, as before, one should perform the binding of the armor with the two index fingers:
"Make all my mudrās firm with the vajra-armor, vaṃ!"
Thus it is said.
In front of the mandala, one should satisfy [the deities] as before.

For the sake of attaining the desired siddhi, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra of Vajrasattva and dedicate the merit. Then, having made the request, "May you forgive whatever deficiency has been committed by me in the ritual," one should offer the *argha*.
And having offered [these], one should urge all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to depart:
*Oṃ, you have accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings; having granted success, go as you please to the realm of the Buddhas, so that you may return again.*
Thus it is said.
And one should release Sattvavajrī from above with this heart-mantra: VAJRASATTVA MUḤ.
Thus [it is said].
In this way, all are dismissed.

Just as the emanated assembly and the collection of wheels were [produced], so too, by means of mental application through skillful yoga, one causes them to enter one's own body using the *vajra-rakṣa*, *yakṣa-sandhi-karma-mudrās*.

Having protected oneself and arisen, one should perform the activities of the mandala, the recitation of the manual, and so forth. In this manner, one should perform these four daily for a month, six months, or a year,
or for as long as one is authorized by the deities.

Alternatively, having performed the great yoga and the worship and so forth as before, one should grasp the vajra with the reality (tattva) and ring the bell with the dharma; then, having empowered the great mudrā with the commitment (samaya), one should recite the heart mantra. // 1 //

(26) Then, reciting the three mantras beginning with *vajrātmaka* and visualizing their respective objects, one should emanate the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm (*vajradhātumahāmaṇḍala*) within the four-seal maṇḍala at one’s own heart using the fivefold Heart-mantra of Protection. Having established Śrī Vairocana and the others in their proper places by means of the previously mentioned heart-mantras, one enters through the yoga of the equality of aspirations. Becoming one with them through the mantras beginning with *vajrātmaka*, one should contemplate oneself as the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm, thinking, "I myself am the Vajra Realm," and [visualize] everything.

Meditating thus, "I am indeed [the deity]," one should recite the heart-mantra of Śrī Vajrasattva. One should also contemplate that the sound of the mantra resonates from the mouths of all the deities. By this very method, all [deities] such as Vairocana and the others are accomplished. When fatigued, one should repeatedly perform the hymn of praise in eight hundred names, the worship, and the four prostrations. At the conclusion of each of the four junctions of the day, having performed the ritual preceded by the hymn of praise in eight hundred names, one should perform the dismissal.

(27) All worldly and supramundane mantras are to be accomplished through Mahāyoga. However, one who is unable to visualize the maṇḍala should perform the Mahāyoga and recite each of all the mantras one hundred thousand times. Having performed one hundred thousand recitations of "Vajrottiṣṭha" and having bound the Vajrottiṣṭha mudrā, he should recite throughout the entire night; thus he becomes accomplished.
(28) From that time forward, with that [mudrā], he should place the flask and other items in the sky.
Firmly joining the two vajra-fingers together and holding them upward.
One should raise up all who are dead by means of that which is designated as "Vajrottiṣṭha. // 1 //
Thus it is said.

Having recited "Vajrāveśa aḥ" one hundred thousand times, and having consecrated the vajra-bell with a thousand oblations of ghee-drops, one should hold it with the Vajrāveśa-samayamudrā and recite throughout the entire night.
By means of that accomplishment, when held in the hand, one causes everything to enter into a state of possession.
Thus [it is said].
Having thus performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should draw the mandala.

To the northeast of the monastery, grove, village, or city, or wherever it may be pleasing to the mind, on a plot of ground that is very level, moist, well-drained, of proper dimensions, and free of saline soil, [one should measure] one hundred cubits or fifty cubits for the king.
For feudal lords and great feudal lords, it should be fifty or twenty-five cubits;
for a merchant chief or a caravan leader, twenty-five or half of that;
for practitioners, twelve or six cubits.

Therein, first of all, having warded off obstacles to the mandala by means of human bone powder mixed with poison in the center of the desired mandala ground, one should perform a pacifying homa for oneself, the disciples, the king, and others; thereafter, one should have the ground purified.
Having dug down to a depth of one fathom, or reaching from the throat to the navel or the knees, and having filled it with fragrant earth that has not been discarded,

one should sprinkle it repeatedly with scented water over which the *vajraśikhara* mantra has been recited, and then strike it. It should be made perfectly level, situated within a gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), and adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*).
It was surrounded by a courtyard with four gates and well-tended on all sides; it was most excellent, with canopies spread out and adorned with hanging bells and auspicious banners;
and it was beautified by images and silk streamers of the Buddha-jewel and others.
Having adorned it with incense burners placed at the four corners,

and having beautified it with flowers, lamps, garments, and so forth, and having smeared it with fragrance and sprinkled it with scented water consecrated by the Vajrayakṣa mantra, one should place the hand upon the ground.
One should recite the Vajrasattva mantra and the hundred-syllable mantra seven times;
this is the procedure for purifying and taking possession of the site.
(31) Then, having bathed himself, with limbs scented with fragrance, wearing ornaments and garments as was fitting,

clothed in well-dyed robes, adorned with garlands, and with a fragrant countenance, beginning from the eighth day of the bright fortnight, or from the tenth, the thirteenth, or the fourteenth, up to the fifteenth—
One should perform the work of the mandala exactly as prescribed.
On a naturally excellent spot of ground, having swept it clean and applied anointment, one should likewise touch it with the hand and cause Vajrasattva to revolve.
Then one should perform the entire ritual procedure;
or alternatively, one may perform it beginning with the forenoon on the full moon day.
On the day of entering the mandala, however, the preceptor, together with the disciple, must remain without food.

Therein, first of all, standing in the center of the great maṇḍala ground, one should perform self-protection, the destruction of obstacles, and so forth. Then, having fashioned the maṇḍala with the vajra-wheel, preceded by prostrations and other rites,
one should accomplish the undertaking of the vows (*saṃvara*), the Mahāyoga, the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), and the seats.
Seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, one should draw oneself [into the visualization]:
"Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life as well;
I shall undoubtedly become equal to the Buddhas of the three times. // 1 //
I shall become irreversible, with a single-minded intent toward awakening;
today my birth in the family of the Tathāgatas will occur, of this there is no doubt. (2)
Today is indeed my foremost day; today my sacrifice is unsurpassed. Today is my supreme assembly, for I have invited all the Buddhas. // 3 //
Thus it is said.
Then, having prostrated with the entire body and holding an incense burner in hand, one should invite all the Buddhas:
"May the Buddhas residing in all directions without exception attend to me!
I, the Vajra-holder named [so-and-so], am fashioning this maṇḍala."
May all the Buddhas and others come; may they bestow this accomplishment. // 1 //
Having said this,
and having visualized the Ādiyoga, the Maṇḍalarājāgrī, and the Karmarājāgrī, one should again, after opening the doors, [worship] with the Great Mudrā of Śrī Vajrasattva in the place of Vajrasattva.

The yogin, established and intent upon the recitation of that mantra, should be requested by the supreme practitioners— who are endowed with the pride of being Tathāgatas— to draw the great maṇḍala with the eight hundred names.
(34) Then, having risen and performed prostrations at the feet of all the Tathāgatas, and seeing that the sky was filled by all the Tathāgatas, [he said]:
"I myself am the Vajra-holder; I myself am Vajrasattva."
I am the Buddha, O Great King; I am the Vajra-holder of great power. // 1 //
I am the King, the Lord of Yogins; I am the firm Vajrapāṇi.
I am the Master, the Great Vajra; through my empowerment, I do not abandon you. // 2 //
(35) Then, the vajra-gaze: *maṭ*.

Having thus placed [the syllables] upon the two eyes, having emanated a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) on the soles of the feet by means of the syllable *aḥ*, and having bound the self-samaya-mudrā, one should raise that maṇḍala into the sky with [the mantra]:
"Vajrasattva, arise! (*vajrasattva uttiṣṭha*).
Thus it is said.
(36) Then, having empowered oneself once with that self-seal (*svasamayamudrā*),
and having again formed the great seal (*mahāmudrā*),
one should likewise rise up and, remaining in the seal, circumambulate while looking all around with pride, uttering "Vajrasattva."

With the vajra-vision, one should create a vajra enclosure and cage consisting of the binding of the boundaries and the mandala, extending from the surface of the earth— held by the soles of the feet— up to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Having again performed the destruction of obstacles and other rites, one should summon the secret-form mandala by means of this [mantra] joined with the mudrā.
Oṃ vajramaṇḍala hūṃ jaḥ.
Thus:
with two vajra-fists, the index fingers and thumbs forming vajras, this is the mudrā named Vajracakrī, which attracts all maṇḍalas.
Oṃ mahā-vajracakrādhitiṣṭha sidhya hūṃ.
Thus, one should consecrate the maṇḍala again with this [mantra];
the Vajrahetukarmamudrā itself is its mudrā.
(37) Then, one should strike with a vajra the four khadira-wood vajra-piles at the four corners of the maṇḍala:
Oṃ vajrakīla kīlaya sarvavighnaṃ bandha hūṃ phaṭ!
Having thus recited this heart-mantra one hundred and eight times,

and having taken up either the left hand in the vajra-fist or a five-pronged vajra, one should produce five stakes at the four corners of the mandala and at its center while uttering the syllable *hūṃ*.
With his right hand, having formed it into a three-pronged vajra, he should strike while uttering this:
*oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ*.
Pierce, pierce all evils, phaṭ!
Vajrakīla, wielder of the vajra, commands: svāhā!
Thus [it is said].

(38) Then, having placed the sprinkling flask consecrated by the Vajrayakṣa mantra at the door of the maṇḍala house, and having strengthened all protections with the Vajramuṣṭi-karmamudrā, one should arm oneself with the Vajrakavaca.
And thus it is said:
One should perform the ritual procedure for binding and yoga, fashion the vajra-fist, and provide protection with the vajra-armour throughout the entire mandala. // 1 //
Thus it is said.
(39) Again, having sat in the center of the mandala and mentally visualized the entire mandala,
one should smear the site of the entire mandala with fragrance.
At the locations of the five Tathāgatas, [one should draw] four squares (caturasrāṇi).
One should prepare mandalas with sandalwood, saffron, and other such substances;
for the remaining [deities], they should be circular. These should be consecrated seven times with their respective mantras.

(40) Then, having drawn [the deities] in with the vajra-hook and other implements, having caused them to enter, bound them, and brought them under control, one should place the Tathāgatas and others from the space of the sky into one’s own heart; having worshipped them with the five types of offerings, one should [place] a small vessel for the consecration, filled with all grains and so forth.

Having cast that [substance] into it, consecrated with the mantra of Vajrasattva, one should perform the ritual consecration (adhivāsana) according to the rules by offering water for honor (argha) with scented water;
and having cast flowers, one should likewise consecrate it with incense.
On another day, however, one should properly recite [the mantra] until the end of the three junctions of the day;
with that which has been further recited, one should perform the consecration in the mandala.
And its characteristic, which will be described hereafter, should be understood by the great-souled ones.
This [substance] should be placed before Śrī Vajrasattva.
Then, one should offer ghee and the other substances individually one hundred and eight times each with the mantras of Vajrayakṣa, Vajrasattva, and Buddhalocanā.
This is the ritual procedure for the preparatory fire offering (*adhivāsana-homa*).
(41) Then, having offered the outer oblation, performed the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśya*), praised [the deity] with the hundred and eight names,
and fully worshipped all the Tathāgatas with flowers and so forth, as well as with dances and other offerings, he should prostrate and prepare the disciples for the consecration.
In that regard, first of all, the master should be provided with those who have bathed well, wear pure garments, and hold flowers in their hands.
Having prostrated, the disciples themselves should say:
"You are my teacher, O Great Hero;
I desire, O Great Lord, the firm method of the Bodhisattvas."
Grant me the commitment; grant me the reality and the bodhicitta. // 1 //
Grant me the Triple Refuge of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
O Protector, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation. // 2 //
Thus it is said.
(42) Thereafter, one should cause [the disciple] to perform the confession of sins and so forth:

"Listen, O you who are composed in the auspicious posture, having properly withdrawn all conceptual constructions! Your expansive mind shall be blessed by the Sugatas, Vajrasattva, and the others. (1)
Whatever unwholesome [deeds] I have committed, approved of, or caused to be done even against my will— all that I now confess before supreme enlightenment.
(2) The two accumulations of the sons of the Sugatas are incessant, unfathomable, and profound.
I rejoice in that which accomplishes the welfare of the entire world, as well as in whatever else [is virtuous].

Out of compassion, I go for refuge to the Sugata, who has destroyed the darkness of delusion with his entire body, whose mind is free from the stain of pride, and who stands at the center of the lotus-like assembly of all noble lineages. (3–4)

I have gone for refuge to the Dharma, which is a garden for those of superior intellect and a "Victor’s Grove" because it strikes fear into the base; it is skillful in dispelling both fear and worldly prosperity,
(5) it removes the venom of the serpents of passion and the like, and possesses a mind of vast compassion and awakened wisdom.
I go for refuge to the host of lords of ascetics, who have transcended existence and are worthy of worship.

(6) Having realized the causes, immediate conditions, dominant factors, objects, self-nature, results, and powers, and having conquered all enemies, I maintain an incomparable realization of awakening, rooted in compassion. (7)
For the sake of maturing sentient beings, or for their protection, and furthermore for the purification of one's own mind, one should give all this away like grass and such. // 1 //
Thus, seeking purity for myself and others, I shall cultivate at every moment ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and unsurpassed wisdom. (2)
In order to lead these worlds to the assembly that is eternally free from the mantras of the Sugatas and flows effortlessly, I now abide here in the celestial realm.
(i) By means of this very root of merit thus fully accomplished, I must become one who relinquishes all that belongs to me;
(ii) I must generate a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
(iii) I must discipline all sentient beings through all vehicles and the full range of all skillful means.
They should be established in the non-abiding realm of nirvāṇa;
furthermore, even after having brought all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa, no sentient being at all has been brought to final nirvāṇa—
thus should I generate the thought.
(v) I must realize the non-arising of all phenomena;
(vi) with an undistracted mind of the wisdom of omniscience, I must train in the six perfections; (vii) I must realize the accomplishment of the single vehicle path.
(ix) I must train myself for the realization and awakening to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;

(ix) I must apply myself to the realization and awakening to the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four types of analytical knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; (x) in this manner, I must practice until the accomplishment of all the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha.

(43) This is that diamond-like production of the great mind of awakening (*mahābodhicittotpāda*) of the Bodhisattvas, the father of all Tathāgatas, the executor of the commands of all Tathāgatas, the eldest son of all Tathāgatas; this is the Blessed One Samantabhadra.
Just so, by me—who am established in the production of the mind and empowered by the roots of merit already accomplished—there is the accomplishment of infinite gateways.
Even when the exposition of the conduct of Samantabhadra has been established and brought to completion,
one should attract, gladden, inspire, and engage the entire multitude of disciples by means of various demonstrations of the different aspects of that conduct.
(44) Then, reciting "samaya āḥ" within the heart of the disciple, one should emanate a moon mandala and, upon it, a five-pronged [vajra].
Having placed the vajra at his heart with [his own] heart, [he says]:
"O Surata, you are the pledge; Hoḥ! O Vajra, accomplish [this] according to your pleasure!
Thus.
Placing his hand, drenched with scented water, upon the head while invoking Vajrasattva, he should contemplate the vajra;
on the forehead, above a moon, the vajra-jewel by means of the syllable TRĀṂ;
and at the throat, the vajra-lotus by means of the syllable HRĪḤ.
At the crown of the head, with the syllable *kaṃ*, is a double-vajra;
[the mantras] are Vajrasattva, Vajraratna, Vajradharma, and Vajrakarma.
Thus one should recite;
one should preside over [the deity] in one's own heart and other locations.
(45) Then, with Vajragandhā, one should place perfume in their hands;
with Puṣpā, flowers;
and with Dhūpā, one should fumigate them.
One should illuminate it with a lamp.

One should provide a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths in length, made of *udumbara* or *aśvattha* wood, smeared with fragrance and tied with a flower at its tip, over which the *vajrahāsa* mantra has been recited.
And with those [fingers], facing either eastward or northward, one should eat the solid food with the tips [of the fingers].
Having given fresh *kuśa* grass over which the *vajratīkṣṇa* mantra has been recited, one should speak thus:
"Having made a mattress with these, and having placed one [blade] upon the head, the bed should be prepared; it should be prepared."
Thus [it is said].
(47) Then, having consecrated it with the Vajrarakṣā mantra, one should oneself bind the cord upon the left hand, provided with three knots, according to the samaya.
(48) Then, having encouraged and gladdened them all with a profound and sublime teaching of the Dharma according to their capacity, he should say:
"Arise, O gentle-faced ones! Tomorrow you shall behold the great maṇḍala."
Thus it is said.
The ritual procedure for acceptance.

(49) Then, at the time of sunrise, having likewise placed that maṇḍala in the sky above, one should mark it out with threads. First, one should prepare threads dyed individually with blue, yellow, red, green, white, and fragrant pigments, and having wound them around a reed, they should be set aside.
HŪṂ TRĀḤ HRĪḤ AḤ ĀḤ //
Having thus placed Akṣobhya and the others upon the threads with these respective seed-syllables, [one should say]:
"O you with the blazing gaze, O goad-holder, JAḤ!"
Having thus performed the placement upon the two eyes,
one should urge Akṣobhya and the others by means of a gaze that draws in the eyelashes of the eyes, which are running and blazing, while reciting this:
"O Blessed One, grant me the vajra-thread for the purpose of laying out the great maṇḍala."
(50) Then, having filled those threads with the light-ray threads of their own seeds sent forth by Akṣobhya and the others— threads drawn in by blazing hooks held in their own hands—
all phenomena follow one another; all phenomena are mutually interpenetrated.
All phenomena are utterly permeated:
Oṃ Vajrasattva Hūṃ.
Having spoken thus, and having formed a circle by joining the two *maṭa* gestures at the right and left eyes to produce the solar and lunar [lights],
and having stabilized them with the "vajra-gaze" while uttering *maṭ*, one should place that thread upon a golden vessel smeared with fragrance or similar surface.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and incense:
Oṃ vajrasamaya sūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ.
Thus it is said.
Having stabilized it with the vajra-bind, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.

(51) Then, having again smeared the mandala ground with fragrance by sixteen practitioners, having adorned it all around with offerings of flowers, having presented the *argha* water to all the families abiding in the intermediate space,
and having fully worshipped them all with flowers and so forth, as well as with the *lāsya* dance and other gestures;

Having prostrated with the syllables *jaḥ* and *kārā*, and having produced the yellow-hued moon and sun in the left and right eyes respectively, one should fashion the mandala together with offerings of the sound of song.
(52) In that regard, first, one should dip a thread previously consecrated with fragrant white pigment into [the liquid].

Then, having become Vairocana by mentally uttering the vajra-speech "Vajradhātu," and pronouncing "Vajrakarma" from one's own heart, one should emanate the northern practitioner in the form of Vajrakarma.

Then Vajrasattva, having proclaimed [the mantra] and visualized himself as Vajrasattva, takes that thread with his left vajra-fist; uttering the syllable *jaḥ*, he dispatches the assistant practitioner— who is the form of Vajrakarma— with the thread in hand,
while contemplating the equality of all directions.
(i) Facing east, one should strike the vajra-thread.
(ii) Again, the preceptor, standing in the south and facing north, [strikes] the second [thread].
(iii) Then, standing in the southeast direction and facing north, [one strikes] the eastern thread of the outer maṇḍala.
(iv) Standing in the northwest, facing south, [he marks] the western line; (v) standing in that very place, [he marks] the northern line;
(vi) again, standing in the southeast quarter, [he marks] the southern side-line and the altar-line.
(vī) Again, standing in the southeast corner, one should recite until reaching the northwest corner;
(vīi) standing in the southwest, one should recite until reaching the northeast corner.
The movement of the preceptor and the superior practitioner should proceed by way of circumambulation.
In this regard, the mantra for the thread is as follows: Oṃ vajrasamaya sūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ.
Thus [it is said].
(53) Jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ.
Thus, with three utterances of the syllable *jaḥ*, the assistant practitioner should perform the drawing of the thread;
the doors shall be one-eighth [of the total size],
and the door-projections shall be equal in measure to the doors.
The altar-railing (*vedikā*) should be half the measure of the door, extending both inside and outside;
the ground for the single-colored powder (*rajobhūmi*) should be half the measure of the altar-railing.
The archway (*toraṇa*) should be made three times the size of the door.

Having laid out the inner mandala as a square, half the size of the outer mandala, surrounded by a platform with four gates and provided with eight pillars, one should place at the center of the mandala a ritual stake (*kīlaka*) made of *khadira* wood,
shaped like a single-pronged vajra at its base and a five-pronged vajra at its top.

As before, having recited the Vajrakīla mantra and struck with the vajra, one should string the vajra-garland from the outside of the inner mandala, starting from this direction and proceeding in a clockwise sequence, using the thread attached to it;
and its length should be double the measurement of the mandala, being six cubits in circumference.
The measurement of the thread should be made according to the smallest [unit], or otherwise, in proportion.

(54) Now, the definition of the sūtra is stated according to the words of the ṛṣis: "The wise one should, according to his ability, mark out the maṇḍala with a new, well-prepared, well-measured, and beautiful sūtra. (1)
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four arches, provided with four lines, and decorated with silk bands, garlands, and strings of flowers. // 2 //
In all the corner sections and at the junctions of the doors and projections,
one should trace the outer mandala, inlaid with vajra-jewels.
Having entered its inner city, which resembles a wheel-less chariot,
it is encircled by a vajra-cord and adorned with eight pillars.
The wise one, maintaining equanimity toward all directions, should lay out the mandala with four lines for the east,
west, north, and south, resulting in eight sections.
Thus.
On the outer and inner vedikās, one should draw necklaces, half-necklaces, chowries, and circles of the moon and sun.
In every corner of the maṇḍala, there should be variegated top-banners with bells suspended and shaken by the wind.
At the junctions of those doors and projections, one should draw vajras and jewel-flames resting upon crescent moons.
Thus...
(55) If one wishes to ward off obstacles,

one should nail down all obstacles by means of invisible stakes— stake-mantras recited one hundred thousand times and consecrated one hundred and eight times— which are placed at the center of the maṇḍala as specified, according to this sequence.
As it has been said: having marked out the circular halo of light for the outer mandala by means of a thread fastened to the pegs situated within the aforementioned mandala, moving clockwise,
one should likewise mark out the circular Cakravāḍa mountain range outside of that.
There, within that circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*), one should fashion images of obstructing deities and others using anthill clay.

In the image of Śakra, situated in his own direction, one should visualize Śakra as yellow by means of the syllable *I*. Likewise, in the elemental nature of Agni and the others, one should visualize Agni as red by means of the syllable *Raṃ*.
"Aham" refers to Yama, who is black;
"kram" refers to the Rākṣasa, who is black;
"vam" refers to Varuṇa, who is white.
Having visualized Vāyu as smoky-colored with the syllable *yam*, Kuvera as yellow with *phaṭ*, and Īśāna as white with *sumbha*;
Having summoned [the obstructors] with the vajra-hook and other implements, having caused them to enter, bound them, and brought them under control, one should nail them down.
If one desires to make [the practice] entirely free from obstacles, they should be covered over with clay.
Even so, if they continue to create obstacles:

Having performed the yoga of Vajrahūṃkāra, having drawn [the obstacle] in with Ṭakkirāja and performed the summoning and so forth with the vajra-hook and other implements, and having bound the Vajrahūṃkāra mudrā, one should step upon the image of the obstacle with the left foot,
saying: *hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ*.
Through such methods of intensification, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, one should from time to time cast that mudrā toward the clouds and other objects,
with the Vajra-hūṃkāra, whose radiance is filled with blazing flames expanding magnificently through the sky.
One should contemplate clouds and the like being reduced to ashes by the impact of blows from one's feet;
in this way, they are destroyed.
Alternatively, having brought the samādhi of emptiness before one's mind, immediately thereafter, with the syllable *A*, [one should perform the same].

Having become Vairocana, one should visualize the form of Vairocana as described in the tantra; then, by means of the syllable *hāṃ*, one should mentally emanate Noble Acala from one's own heart with the mantra:
*vajra hāṃ bandha*.

Thus, mentally reciting this, one should create seven drops of perfume in the northwestern corner outside the outer mandala; having internalized each individual drop with the syllable *yaṃ*, one should place the seventh *yaṃ* syllable, joined with a drop (*bindu*), in the center.

These seven drops are the seven winds, the lords of beasts, black in color; they are to be visualized as bound and brought by the noose of Noble Acala. In their midst is one leader, and the remaining six drops are situated surrounding him on all sides.
Then, having visualized Mount Meru in the form of a shallow bowl (śarāva), one should visualize above it the mandala of Mahendra in the very same form, entirely covered with vajras;
and in its center, a five-pronged vajra, seeded with the syllable *hūṃ*.
Having visualized tridents in the corners,
likewise recite: *vajra hāṃ bandha*.
Uttering this, one should drink the seven drops as previously described using that bowl.

Then, having visualized the aforementioned Lord Vairocana upon the Meru-mountain atop the bowl by means of the syllable *Aṃ*, and [having visualized] Noble Acala with his legs in the *ālīḍha* posture, pressing down upon the mountain, the Lords—
One should visualize [the deity] in front, holding a sword and a noose in his hands and threatening the wind;
in this way, the binding of all winds is accomplished.
(58) It serves to ward off obstacles such as water from below and so forth.

Having manifested oneself as Āryācala, situated upon the wind and fire mandalas by means of the syllable *hāṃ*, one should fashion an image of the obstacle-maker (*vighna*) out of anthill earth or fallen cow dung;
then, having produced a sword with the syllable *khaṃ* and the letter *ra* containing fire within it.

Having produced the noose and the hook-samaya with the syllable *kṣmī*, taking them with the left hand and holding a sword with the right, one should draw [the obstacle] in with the noose and establish him within the nature of the obstacle.
Standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, one should press down upon his head with the left foot while uttering this:
Homage to all Vajras! O Caṇḍamāroṣaṇa, shatter it! HŪṂ TRAṂ HĀṂ MĀṂ!
Thus it is said.
One should either tear that effigy apart with a sword,
or, having smeared the effigy with mustard seeds soaked in poison, one should heat it over a fire.
For he has been scorched by fire and smeared with [poison], there is no doubt;
even one who is a Brahmā or even Śakra would be consumed instantly at that very moment.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Vairocana.
(59) Having performed ten thousand recitations (*ayutasevā*) of this mantra through the yoga of Noble Acala, one should thereafter perform the ritual action.
With the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, one should [visualize] Noble Mañjuśrī as Māntaka, black in color and six-legged.

Having visualized [the deity] with four faces and four arms, holding a sword and an axe in his two right hands and a noose and a mace in his two left hands, facing southward, and filling the sky with hosts of wrathful deities, one should form the trident mudrā and employ it forcefully to ward off clouds and other such obstacles.
In the *talavajrabandha* (the vajra-binding of the palms), the two index fingers are extended like needles; this is the *śūlamudrā*.

If even by this means the pacification of obstacles does not occur, [one should perform the rite] with blood, cemetery charcoal, poison, *rājika* mustard seeds, and the juice of *unmattaka* and *pattūra* between two unbaked earthenware bowls.

Having written the mantra and placed white mustard seeds over which one hundred and eight recitations have been performed into that pair of shallow earthen bowls, and having observed the fire and any obstacles, one should offer a hundred or seven oblations;
then they will either perish, die, or be seized by non-human beings.

Alternatively, having performed one hundred thousand recitations of the syllable *hūṃ* through the yoga of Vajrahūṃkāra, one should likewise attract [the deity] with the vajra-hook and other implements, cause [him] to enter, bind [him], and nail the effigy with a stake made of human bone measuring four finger-breadths in length, over which one hundred and eight recitations have been performed, using the vajra.
(60) Now, the pacification of the burning by fire is described:

above the fire, by means of the syllable *vaṃ*, there is a mandala of Varuṇa; above that, a wheel situated in the center of a lotus; and above that, by means of the syllable *vaṃ* once again, Vairocana, white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon.
One should visualize [the deity] seated, filling the ten directions with nine streams of water resembling the four oceans, the four rivers, and the Anavatapta lake;
and with the Vajra-eye, the Vajra-flame, the Fire-sun, and the Śarāva, one should [fix] Meru as a stake.
And having protected [the area] with the two eyes of Vajrayakṣa and Vajrabhairava, one should effect a binding of space over them and provide a vajra-cage by means of the vajra-binding;
or else, one should perform the warding off of obstacles through an *abhicāra* fire-oblation.
(61) Then, having uprooted the stake situated at the center of the mandala with the four *hūṃ* syllables,
one should fill the pit of the stake with the five colors to be described and level it.
Then, having produced the moon and sun in the left and right eyes with the syllable *hrīḥ*,...
Having gazed all around with a wrathful look, he should close the doors.
(62) Then, there is the consecration of the stage:
Oṃ vajracitrasamaya hūṃ.
"By means of this [mantra] joined with the mudrā, one should consecrate all the limbs seven times;
they become composed of vajra," so said the Blessed One, the Great Vajradhara.
In this regard, this is the mudrā:
Having joined the two tips of the two vajra-mudrās together very firmly, one should summon all the deities with a blazing gaze. // 1 //
(63) At the end, with the syllable *hīḥ* and the Vajrasūryakrodha-samayamudrā, one should cause it to blaze with the left vajra-fist.
*Oṃ vajracitrasamaya hūṃ*.
Uttering this, one should cast the colored powder (*raṅga*) clockwise around the mandala, beginning from the northeastern direction.
Thereafter, as is convenient, one should draw the lines in this sequence: blue, yellow, red, dark green, and white.
The measurement for the smallest [mandala] is six cubits.
But with the increase of the hand, there is an increase of the foot;
and so it is said in the *Vajraśekhara*:
"The needle made of blue vajra has a supreme golden support."
"The needles are made of ruby, and another is made of emerald;
they should be known as white on the inside—this is remembered as the sequence of colors.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Mahāvajradhara.
The eastern side is deep blue, the southern is endowed with yellow,
the western part is red, and the northern is endowed with madder-red.
In the center, one should always draw a supreme ground-section with the luster of crystal, while remaining well-composed and holding a vajra and bell. // 2 //
Within those situated at the tips of the vajra spokes and adorned with five mandalas, one should place the image of the Buddha in the center of the central mandala. // 3 //
On all sides of the Buddha, in the center of the mandalas,
one should indeed draw the four supreme commitments in successive order.
Having entered by means of the Vajravega [mudrā] into the fourfold mandalas, one should establish the four Buddhas, beginning with Akṣobhya, within them. (5)
One should construct the Akṣobhya maṇḍala together with Vajradhara and the others;
the Ratnasaṃbhava maṇḍala is filled with Vajragarbha and the others. (6)
The auspicious mandala of Amitāyus should be drawn by Vajranetra and the others; likewise, the mandala of Amoghasiddhi, beginning with the Vajra-viśva, should be drawn.
Thus it is said.
One should draw the Vajra goddesses situated at the corners of the wheel;
one should likewise draw the Buddha offerings at the corners of the outer maṇḍala. // 8 //
In the middle of all the doors, one should place the four door-keepers;
among those situated on the outer mandala, one should establish the Great Beings (mahāsattvas).
In this regard, this is the heart-mantra of Vajravega:
Oṃ vajravegākrama hūṃ.
Thus it is said.
Now, his mudrā is as follows:
having mentally raised a line, just like a vajra-thread, whether entering or exiting, he does not fall away from the samaya. // 10 //
Thus it is said.

(65) Therein, the Blessed One Vairocana is white in color, seated upon a lion throne in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, holding a five-pronged vajra with the bodhyagrī mudrā, possessing solar radiance, and wearing a lower garment and upper robe of fine silk.
He has four faces; he faces east with his principal face, wears a jeweled crown, and is consecrated with the silk ribbon.

In this way, Akṣobhya and the others are likewise seated upon elephant-thrones in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, with solar halos, facing Vairocana, and receiving the consecration of the jeweled crown and ribbon; their colors are blue, yellow, red, and dark green, respectively.

Having single faces and holding a five-pronged vajra, a vajra-jewel, a lotus, a wheel, and a double-vajra (viśvavajra) [in their right hands], they are accompanied by their respective great mudrās (mahāmudrās).
While reciting the heart-mantra of the five Tathāgatas, "Vajradhātu," they should be established or drawn;
and those residing in the intermediate space should likewise be brought down and unified [with the visualized forms].
(66) Thus [is] Sattvavajrī;
thus [it continues] up to Sattvavajrī.
"Varāveśa aḥ"—
thus is the vajrāveśa.
Before the Blessed One Vairocana is Sattvavajrī, holding a five-pronged red vajra.
On the right side is the Cintāmaṇiratna with a five-pronged vajra at its peak;
behind it is a lotus with sixteen petals, white and red,
eight of whose petals are turned downward.
And above, [upari cā]...

Having consecrated oneself with that water, at the time of entry, one should bind the disciple with the Vajrasattva-vajrī [mudrā],
or cause him to bind it.
As for the vases of Śrī-Vairocana and the others, each should be placed outside the outer maṇḍala, marked with its own respective insignia.

Then, having performed the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth, immediately after [the recitation of] "I am the Vajra of Rapture" (*suratavajra*) and so on—
Having uttered the name and bound the great mudrā of Vairocana, at that location [one recites]:

And thus, having finally perfected one's own heart-mantras, one should consecrate the Tathāgatas and others, up to those of the Fortunate Aeon, with the consecrations of mudrās, by means of the Dharma, Karma, and Mahāmudrās, and by means of the mudrā-consecrations.

In that regard, for Sattvavajra and the others, their own heart-mantras (*svahṛdaya*) are the dharma-mudrās. For Vajrasattva, Ratna, Dharma, and Karma, there are both karma-mudrās and mahāmudrās; these are the female forms contained within the [mandalas of] Vajra and the rest, appearing in the forms of Vajrasattva and the others.
Having turned the left *tathāgata-muṣṭi* palm upward, one should extend the little finger with the index finger and thumb of the right hand and form the hollowed *añjali*.
This is the *samaya-mudrā* of Maitreya and the others, and their *vidyā* is as previously stated.
One should place that very vidyā upon their tongues; this is their Dharma-mudrā.

Having generated a double vajra in one's own heart with the syllable *aḥ*, and having formed the great seals (*mahāmudrā*) according to their respective drawings, they become action seals (*karmamudrā*).
Having visualized a five-pronged vajra in one's own heart according to the [prescribed] drawing, their great mudrās (mahāmudrā) should be bound;
and this very vidyā is common [to all].
Then, having offered the *argha* water, one should perform worship with ten thousand, one thousand, six hundred, or even just one pair of garments for each [deity].
Or [one may prepare] a universal canopy of various kinds,

with variegated banners suspended at its four corners; and having consecrated the parasols and banners seven times with the syllable Oṃ and Vajrasattva, one should [arrange] a hundred flowering trees or four trees.
And having consecrated all the flowers as before with "Oṃ vajrasphara khaṃ," [one should offer them].
Thus one should offer it.

With the *gandhavidyā*, one should consecrate all perfumes, incenses, and fragrant ointments; and with the *dhūpavidyā*, one should consecrate camphor, *agaru*, *turuṣka*, and sandalwood mixed with other [substances]. One should burn a hundred thousand, ten thousand, a thousand, or a hundred incense sticks, but never less than ten.
One should prepare a thousand, a hundred, ten, or four lamp-vessels containing ghee-lamps and so forth, numbering one hundred thousand or more; having consecrated them as before with the lamp-mantra.

Having first performed the svastika rite, one should present an offering of oblations (*balyupahāra*) consisting of one hundred thousand, ten thousand, one hundred, or ten units of coins, as well as various kinds of edible foods, exactly as before. One should dedicate these to all the deities with the mantra beginning "A-kāro mukhyaḥ," and so forth.

Ten thousand musical instruments, in the form of ten types of instruments, are played with the mudrās of instrumental music, using the vajra-fists or the fingers of the hands in the performance of instrumental music. These ten types are as follows: the lute (*vīṇā*), flute (*vaṃśa*), drum (*muraja*), *mukunda* drum, gong (*kāṃsi*), *bherī* drum, *mṛdaṅga* drum, kettle-drum (*paṭaha*), the *guñjati* instrument, and the performance of the *milā* instrument. [This applies to] instrumental music, actors, dancers, crowns, bracelets, earrings, and so forth.
And the banners should be consecrated with the syllable *oṃ* or the syllable *hūṃ* and then lowered.

Likewise, a cloth banner should be prepared, adorned with garlands and chowries, decorated with necklaces and half-necklaces, and graced by the shape of a crescent moon. Well-prepared herds of horses, elephants, and cattle should also be offered.
And there were beautiful archways, equipped with bells and other ornaments.
Then, having performed worship with Vajralāsyā and the others, one should make the request to all the Tathāgatas: "Act for the benefit of all sentient beings and for the sake of all accomplishments."
Then, having established the northern practitioner within the mandala, one should offer the external oblation (bali) together with parched grain,
sesame seeds, water, cooked rice, and flowers.
Having recited the mantra over snacks such as *śaṣkulikā* and so forth, beginning with the syllable *cā*. // 1 //
Beginning from the eastern direction, one should cast three [offerings]. One should present perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and water for the guest (argha) both at the beginning and at the end.
In that regard, one should first have the mandalas prepared;
thereafter, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana).
Then one should show the pledge (samaya),
and having offered the water of honor (argha) and worshipped with perfumes and so forth, one should present the sacrificial offering (bali).
After that, one should dismiss [the deity].
In this regard, these are the mudrās and mantras:
Śakra stands with the *ālīḍha* posture, facing east;
he should display the left vajra and, holding the right vajra at the region of his hip, he should summon [the deity] with the hook of the right index finger.
The *samayamudrā* of Śakra is [formed] without the index-finger hook (*tarjany-aṅkuśa*).
Standing in the *prayālīḍha* posture, one extends the index finger of the *āvāhanamudrā* to form the *visarjanamudrā*.
Now, his mantra is as follows:
Homage to Vajra! O Vajrapāṇi, protect, protect in every direction, svāhā!
Having bent the right index finger into the shape of a ring and holding it at the third joint of the middle finger like a needle, one should place the thumb in the center of the palm;
this is the mudrā for the invocation of Agni.

The *samaya-mudrā* of Agni is formed by resting the thumb and index finger against the sides [of the palms] in the *āvāhana-mudrā*. The *visarjana-mudrā* is formed by joining the nails of the thumb and index finger together, facing each other, within the center of this very same hand.
The mantra: O Agni, come! O Ākapila, O Kapila, blaze forth, blaze forth! Burn! O Śikhidhūli, O Virūpākṣa, svāhā!
Facing Yama, the practitioner should place both hands facing each other and perform the inner vajra-bind (*abhyantaravajrabandha*);
with the pair of thumbs joined in the center and the two ring fingers forming a needle-pointing outward, one should again hold them inward— this is the invocation mudrā of Yama.
Furthermore, having likewise formed a needle with the ring finger on the outside, one should hold the mudrā at the heart; this is the *samayamudrā*.
With this very needle of the ring finger, the dismissal (*visarjana*) is performed.
The mantra:
Svāhā to Yama!
[Nairṛti], facing the southwest, stands with feet together; having made a fist with the right hand, he should bend the middle and index fingers,
positioning them in the shape of a sword, and should hold the left hand at the region of the hip.
Bending the left index finger constitutes the invocation mudrā of Nairṛti.
With this very same mudrā, placing the left hand at the region of the hip forms the sword mudrā, which is the commitment (samaya) mudrā of Nairṛti.
The dismissal mudrā is formed by extending the index finger of the invocation mudrā.
The mantra is:
*sarvabhūtabhayaṃkara kuru 2 svāhā*.
Facing the western direction with both feet placed evenly, one should join the index finger and thumb of the right hand together.
Holding the left fist at the heart, one should invoke [the deity] with the hook of the left index finger;
this is the mudrā for the invocation of Varuṇa.
From this very [mudrā], one should hold the left index finger by means of the fist-union; this is the noose-mudrā (pāśamudrā), the pledge-mudrā (samayamudrā) of Varuṇa.
For the invocation-mudrā, one extends the index finger; for the dismissal-mudrā, [the same]. The mantra is: [mantra].
tṛ tṛ puṭ tṛ tṛ śikhitoli virūpākṣa svāhā!
Standing facing the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), one should release the middle finger of the left hand as a needle and join the index finger at its third joint in the shape of a coil;
extending it forward while placing the right hand on the hip with the thumb bent constitutes the *āvāhana-mudrā* for Vāyu.
The *samayamudrā* of Vāyu is formed with this same [mudrā] as before, using the thumb.
By extending the thumb of the *āvāhanamudrā*, it becomes the *visarjanamudrā*. The mantra is:
Oṃ śvasa khākha khākha svāhā!
Standing facing the north, having brought both hands forward, one should perform the inner vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*),
with the two little fingers extended like needles and the pair of ring fingers behind them.
Holding each [finger] separately, one should bend the middle finger into the shape of a vajra; this is the *mudrā* for the invocation of Kubera.
From the same *mudrā*, by means of the internal vajra-binding (*vajrabandha*), one should place the two middle fingers together; this is the *samaya-mudrā* of Kubera.
The dismissal mudrā (*visarjanamudrā*) consists of extending both middle fingers from the invocation mudrā (*āvāhanamudrā*).
The mantra is: *oṃ kuberāya svāhā*.
In the northeastern direction, standing facing that [deity], one should join both hands together in *añjali* and form the *talavajrabandha* with the little fingers and ring fingers;
the pair of thumbs should rest upon the middle fingers, while the middle finger-tips are positioned externally in the shape of a *vajra*.
Having placed the two index fingers and then bending them upward so that their nails are joined to one another, this is the mudrā for the invocation of Īśāna.
Holding the two index fingers of this very same mudrā in the form of a vajra as before constitutes the samaya-mudrā of Īśāna.
The mantra: Oṃ juṃ juṃ Śiva svāhā.

Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, holding the two hands in the form of a *añjali* and looking upward, one performs the invocation of Brahmā and the other gods by means of the hook of the two index fingers.
Keeping the two index fingers of this very same mudrā positioned as before, it becomes the *samaya-mudrā*.
The dismissal mudrā is formed by extending both index fingers from the invocation mudrā. The mantras are as follows:
Svāhā to the Brahman above!
Svāhā to Sūrya, the lord of the planets! Svāhā to Candra, the lord of the lunar mansions!
Standing with the feet together on the ground, joining the two hands together so that the fingertips are slightly separated from one another,
and forming the thumbs into a circular shape while casting the gaze downward, one performs the invocation of the elements, beginning with earth, by means of the index fingers acting as hooks.
Having positioned the two index fingers as before, this is the *samaya-mudrā*.
The dismissal is performed with the two index fingers extended from the *āvāhana-mudrā*.
The mantras are as follows:
Svāhā to that which is below the earth!
Svāhā to the Asuras! Svāhā to the Nāgas!

Thus, having given the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) to everyone there with their respective mantras, and having said, "May you grant me the accomplishment of my rites without obstacles," he should dismiss them all along with his circle of disciples.
Then, one should offer the bali-oblation with the verses recited by Subāhu:
"O gods, asuras, all serpents, and siddhas..."
The Tārkṣyas, Suparṇas, and Kaṭapūtanas; the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and whatever classes of Grahas there may be—those who dwell upon the earth and those who are divine. (1)
With one knee placed upon the surface of the earth and palms joined in reverence, I address them,
together with their sons, wives, and hosts of servants.
Having heard this, may they come here for the sake of bestowing grace. // 2 //
Those beings who dwell on the summit of Meru, those in the Nandana grove and in the abodes of the gods,
and those who are on Udaya and Mandara;
And those who dwell in all the cities. // 3 //
They have made their dwellings in all rivers and at their confluences, as well as in places abounding in jewels,
and in large and small ponds and pools.
In the caves, on the embankments, and at the waterfalls. // 4 //
Those who are in a village or a hamlet, or in a beautiful grove, or in an empty dwelling or a temple;
those who are in monasteries, shrines, lodgings, or hermitages.
And in the stables and the sheds for the elephants. // 5 //
Those who dwell in the painted palaces of kings,
and those who dwell in streets, alleys, crossroads, at solitary trees, and on great highways;
In the great cremation grounds and in the great forests. // 6 //] — — —
