(68) ... Then, having bound the *samaya-mudrā* of the Vajra-entrance together with a bell,

and having stepped upon his right foot with one’s left foot, one should visualize Vairocana above in the space over Śrīvajrasattva, being assailed by a mass of rays from the wrathful syllable *HŪṂ* for the purpose of entering into him.
And from below, it is raised up by the *hūṃ* syllable from the circle of vajra-winds;
likewise by Akṣobhya and the others situated in the directions of the east and so forth:
*hūṃ trāḥ hrīḥ aḥ*.
Thinking that he is being showered down by these arrays of light rays from his own seed-syllables, one should cause him to enter [the mandala] with:
Vajrasattva aḥ aḥ aḥ aḥ.
Thus, one should repeat it in that very same way.
(69) Now, if because of the abundance of evil no possession occurs, then one should repeatedly burst open his evils with the *pāpasphoṭana* mudrā.
Having kindled the fire with sweet-smelling sacrificial wood (*samidh*), being well-composed, [one should proceed].
Indeed, by means of an oblation of sesame seeds, all his sins shall be utterly consumed. // 1 //
Oṃ, svāhā to the vajra that burns away all sins!

Thus, having fashioned an effigy of sin with black sesame seeds on the palm of the right hand and visualizing the syllable *hūṃ* in its center, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) using the index finger and thumb.
Then, one should visualize that, having emerged from the *homakuṇḍa*, the sins [of the disciple] are being burned by vajras wreathed in garlands of flames; thus, [the deity] will certainly enter him.
Even so, for one who does not undergo this possession (*āveśa*), one should not perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
And for one who is thus possessed, the accomplishment of the five superknowledges and so forth occurs from that very moment.
Then, having recognized that [the disciple] was possessed, the preceptor says:
"O Vajrasattva! O Vajraratna! O Vajradharma! O Vajrakarma!"
Thus, having bound the Samayamudrā of Vajrasattva, it should be recited: "Furthermore,
O Nṛtyasattva, O Nṛtyavajra!"
Thus it is said.
If he is possessed, he should bind the mudrā of Śrī Vajrasattva;
then the preceptor should display the vajra-fist mudrā.
In this way, all [deities] beginning with Śrī Vajrasattva will manifest their presence.
Then, having visualized a vajra upon the tongue of that person who has been possessed, one should ask about the desired object with these words:
"Speak, O Vajra!"
Thus it should be said;
then he speaks everything.
(71) Then, one should cast that garland into the great maṇḍala, saying: "Accept it, O Vajra! Hoḥ!
Thereafter, wherever it falls, that [deity] will be accomplished for him.
Then one should bind that garland upon his very head, saying:
"Oṃ, accept this, O being of great power!"
Thus it is said.
(72) Then, one should release the binding of the face with this:
*Oṃ vajrasattvaḥ svayaṃ te 'dya cakṣūdghāṭanatatparaḥ*.
The one with all-seeing eyes opens the unsurpassed vajra-eye. // 1 //
(73) Then, one should show the great maṇḍala, beginning with Vajrāṅkuśa and ending with Vairocana. Then:
"Tathāgata, remain, O Vajra!"
With these and other such words, one should cause the release of the entrance-mudrā into the heart of the disciple.
Then, having drawn a moon-maṇḍala either inside the outer maṇḍala facing the eastern gate, or on the outside;
Having established the disciple upon a moon mandala by means of the four mudrās beginning with Sattvavajrī and his own samaya-mudrā, one should consecrate him;
having honored him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having offered the argha water,
[one should do so] with umbrellas, banners, flags, and the like, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and conchs.

Then, having offered congratulations with auspicious verses, one should first consecrate [the disciple] with the water-consecration, the crown-and-ribbon consecration, and the consecration of the name of the Vajra-Lord; furthermore, one should worship him with flowers and other offerings, as well as with the eightfold worship beginning with *lāsya*. Then, by the disciple—
Having given the supreme dakṣiṇā and having prostrated again and again to the ācārya, one should receive the empowerments of flowers and so forth with the *valitavajra* añjali;
however, the ācāryābhiṣeka should be established by means of the great mudrā of Śrī Vajrasattva.
In the locations as previously specified, having projected Śrī Vajrasattva and the others onto his body by means of the *samayamudrās*,
and having installed an image of Śrī Vajrasattva upon his head, one should bestow the water initiation and recite this mantra one hundred and eight times.
Oṃ mahāsukha vajrasattva jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ, you are the one who delights in bliss. Thus.
Then, having performed all the rites, having praised [the disciple] with eight hundred names of disciples,
and having granted permission with five verses, one should prophesy for all the disciples by means of the prophecy of the *udgāthā*.

(75) Now follows the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*). [The master] should instruct [the candidate], who is worthy of the master’s initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), in all ritual activities (*sarvakarma*). By this much, one becomes initiated through the secret initiation.
Thus is the concise procedure.

(76) Leaving a space of exactly two cubits from the root mandala, one should draw a square mandala facing the entrance door, measuring half the size of the inner mandala, with five colored powders, having its western door; in the center of that [square], an eight-petalled lotus.

Above that, one should draw a five-pronged vajra, red in color and garlanded with rays of light. Then, having worshipped that maṇḍala with flowers and other offerings, one should place upon it a lion throne or a pedestal covered by a cloth depicting a moon-maṇḍala, consecrated with the Vajrayakṣa mantra as previously described.

Having empowered the disciple as Vajrasattva and established him there with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Vajrasattva, one should arrange a canopy over the lion throne. On the right side, there should be a white parasol topped with a crest-jewel, adorned with cloth garlands and strings of flowers, consecrated with the mantra *hūṃ*. On the left side, there should be various cloths and variegated banners and flags.

Having consecrated them with the Gaganagañja mantra, established them, offered the *argha*, and worshipped them with flowers and other offerings; and having played musical instruments such as the conch, the *paṭaha*, the *bherī*, and the *kāhala*— which are empowered by the instrumental mudrās—
and with instrumental music, dance, and song, including the *vajralāsya* and others, while taking the supreme sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having installed an image of Śrī Vajrasattva upon his head, one should recite the verses of auspiciousness.

May that Buddha—who possesses the splendor of Mount Meru, who is the lord of the three worlds, who has abandoned the three impurities, and whose eyes are like the petals of a blossomed lotus—grant you auspiciousness and peace today. (1)

Thus instructed was the Preeminent One, immovable, renowned throughout the three worlds, honored by men and gods, the supreme Dharma that brings peace to all beings; in this world, that is the second auspicious blessing. (2)
Endowed with the true Dharma, rich in the auspiciousness of learning, the Saṅgha is worthy of offerings from humans, gods, and asuras;
it is the abode of modesty and glory, the most excellent among assemblies—this is the third auspicious blessing in the world. (3)

Whatever auspiciousness there was when the Tathāgata descended here from the supreme palace of the Tuṣita gods for the benefit of the world, accompanied by the deities led by Indra—may that auspiciousness bring you peace today. (4)

Whatever auspiciousness there was at the birth of the Lord, the ender of existence, in the lovely Lumbinī grove—filled with blossoming sprouts and flowers, and frequented by many gods—may that same auspiciousness bring you peace today. (5)
In the royal palace of the city of Kapilavastu,
may there be the auspiciousness of the birth from the womb of the Teacher, the Sugata, the Son of Sudāna,
who was swiftly nurtured by the waters of nectar.
By this auspiciousness, may there be peace for all living beings. 6.

Whatever auspiciousness belonged to the Tathāgata of infinite merit—who was praised and venerated by the high-souled gods in the supreme city called Kapila—may that auspiciousness bring you peace today. (7)
Whatever auspiciousness there was for you as you joyfully departed for the forest of asceticism at midnight—
surrounded by the gods and receiving their salutations— may that same auspiciousness bring you peace today. (8)

Whatever auspiciousness there was for the Sage—who delights in the jewel of the True Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all beings and who possesses vast prowess in the accomplishment of all goals—may that auspiciousness bring you peace today. (9)

Whatever auspiciousness belongs to him whose body is like blazing gold, who sits amidst a bed of grass the color of beryl, firmly bound in the cross-legged posture and utterly motionless— may that auspiciousness bring you peace today. (10)
May that auspiciousness which was honored by the king of nāgas— the one who utterly eliminates existence and is surrounded by a garland of kuśa grass on the bank of the river— be with you.
By this auspiciousness, may there be peace for all living beings! 11.
Whatever auspiciousness there was when the Blessed One, by the power of loving-kindness, conquered the hosts of Māra at the foot of the king of trees—
whether it occurred on the earth or in the sky in various ways— may that auspiciousness bring you peace today. 12.
Having sat upon the Vajra Seat for the sake of ending all suffering,
at the break of dawn he subdued the four Māras;
may that be the auspiciousness of the Teacher, the Sugata.
By this auspiciousness, may there be peace for all living beings! 13.
Whatever auspiciousness there was when the Teacher, having arrived at Vārāṇasī, proclaimed the sublime Wheel of Dharma—
wonderful and manifest both upon the earth and in the sky— may that auspiciousness bring you peace today. (14)

Whatever auspiciousness is beneficial, supreme, pure, a source of meritorious action, and cherished by noble beings—the Blessed One, the Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, proclaimed that entirely; may that auspiciousness bring you peace today. 15.
This is the auspicious benediction of the King who displays the supreme miracles in order to humble the pride of all heretics and to bring about the welfare of wandering beings.
By this auspiciousness, may there be peace for all living beings. 16.
For the benefit of wandering beings, you have come here to this celestial realm;
may there be the auspiciousness of being completely surrounded by the gods, such as the Ṛṣis, who hold fly-whisks, parasols, and various other offerings in their hands.
By this auspiciousness, may there be peace for all living beings! // 17 //
The auspiciousness of the Tathāgata, who has arrived at the supreme peace,
who is honored with many māndārava flowers, and who is praised by the supreme gods— may that auspiciousness [be present].
By this auspiciousness, may there be peace for all living beings. 18.

Having first praised [the deity] with the eight hundred names, and while reciting the heart-mantras of Vajrāṅkuśa and the others, one should then take water from those vases— specifically from the *vijaya*-vase using the *vajramuṣṭi* [mudrā]— and having bestowed both the consecration and the drinking, one should perform the water-consecration (*udakābhiṣeka*) by means of the vase. The procedure for this is as follows:
Vajrāṅkuśa, Oṃ vajrābhiṣiñca! ... up to ... Oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ! Oṃ vajrābhiṣiñca! Oṃ mahāsukha!
One should repeat this and so forth as before; the remainder is exactly as previously described.
This is the middle stage.

(79) Now follows the procedure for the extensive consecration (*vistarābhiṣeka*). Having performed everything as before, one should worship with the eightfold ritual of worship beginning with *lāsya*. Then, taking either a rod of coral or a golden rod, and standing before [the deity], one should speak these words with clear speech:
O child, the veil of ignorance has been removed from you by the Victors, just as the darkness of the world is removed by the king of physicians with his probe. (1)
Then his heart [mantra]: Oṃ vajranetrāpahara paṭalaṃ hrīḥ.
Thus it is said.
Then, taking up a mirror, he should explain the characteristics of phenomena:
"Phenomena are like reflections; they are transparent, pure, and indeed unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet they arise from causes and karma. // 1 //
Having thus understood that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and without abode, accomplish the incomparable welfare of all; you have been born upon the breast of the Protectors.
Thus [it is said].
[Then, taking up the bell, ring it:
(The characteristic of space) All things have the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics.
Through the union with the equality of space, the equality of all that is supreme is manifest. // 3 //
Thus it is said.
One should offer the bell. *Aḥ* is the essence-mantra for offering the bell.
Then, one should cast four arrows in the four directions with the mantra *sarvatathāgatārāgayasva*. With one [arrow], it should be directed upward; and downward, *hoḥ*.
Again, taking up a mirror, he should speak thus:
"Like a mirror, O Vajrasattva, you are transparent, pure, and indeed unclouded;
the Lord of all Buddhas himself abides in your heart, my child. (4)
Thus it is said.
And it should be said: "Understand that this Bodhicitta is the sovereign of all Tathāgatas.
Then, for his taking up of the mirror, the mantra is:
*Ā vajrasattva*.
Thus it is said.
Then, having placed the wheel of Dharma between his feet and having placed a conch shell in his right hand, he should speak thus:
"From this day forward, by the mere raising of the mind, you shall set in motion the wheel of Dharma."
Having completely filled the unsurpassed Dharma-conch from all sides. // 1 //
But you, with a mind free from doubt and hesitation, should always proclaim in the world this method of the practice of mantra. // 2 //
Thus you are celebrated as one who knows gratitude and is a benefactor to the Buddhas;
and all those Vajradharas protect you from every side. (3)
Thus [it is said].
The two vajra-wheels, conjoined with the syllables of the Dharma, should be employed;
furthermore,
for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, everywhere and in all worlds.
May the wheel of Dharma be turned for the sake of the world according to discipline. // 4 //
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way, may the universal vajra-wheel turn according to the needs of those to be trained. // 5 //
"In this way, may the wheel of the Wrathful Lotus-Jewel be set in motion"—with these five verses, one should grant permission.
Then, with his own verse, he should indeed prophesy [the disciple] as a Tathāgata—[a being] whose entire self-nature consists of all Buddhas—by means of the Vajra-name consecrations:
*Oṃ, I hereby prophesy you: you are the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, [liberated] from the miserable states of existence.*
Having utterly uprooted existence, may one attain accomplishment. O Tathāgata named Vajra, accomplish!
You are the pledge; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ!
Thus [it is said].

In this regard, there is this verse: having formed two *tathāgatamuṣṭi* fists, one performs the gesture of holding the corner of the upper robe with the left hand, and with the right, the gesture of granting boons (*varadāna*).
Thereafter, it should be explained to the disciples in this manner.

For one who receives the prophecy regarding the supreme secret ritual through this great mudrā of the *udgāthā*, all the Tathāgatas, such as Vajrasattva and the rest, together with the assembly circle of all the Bodhisattvas who hold the vajra, and in unison with their own master of the pledge (*samaya-ācārya*), [proclaim] the unsurpassed...
He grants the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Thus,
he bestows the empowerment of the supreme secret siddhi of the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) and the mantras.
It should be understood that "kyi" is a particle used for emphasis. As for the remaining details regarding the inhalation of breath, they should be learned from the *Śrīparamādya*.
(83) Then, one should indeed train all [disciples] in the secret gnosis of the maṇḍala:
"There is no evil equal to dispassion for sentient beings within the three realms;
therefore, you must never again cultivate detachment from desire. (1)
O Great Assembly, slay! Phaṭ!
Thus one should recite this Great Pledge Mantra (*mahāsamayamantra*).
Then, having bestowed the mantra, one should instruct [the disciple] in the knowledge of the four mudrās of one’s own deity. This should be spoken according to this procedure:
"You must not teach even a single one of these mudrās to anyone else who is unskilled in them."

The mudrā should be displayed. Why is that? Because those beings, having not seen the great maṇḍala, employ the binding of the *sattva*-mudrā; at that time, their accomplishment will not be such [as it should be]. Consequently, due to their falling into doubt and failing to avoid irregularity, [they will fail].
Having died very soon, they would fall into the great Avīci hell; you would thus go to a state of sin.
Thus [it is said].

Then, having worshipped all the Tathāgatas with the eightfold worship beginning with *lāsya* and with flowers and so forth, he should inform all the Tathāgatas, saying, "May everyone worship according to their ability. Having thus requested the Tathāgatas, he should have them perform worship with incense and other offerings as they desire, in the order in which they entered.

Having satisfied [the deities] according to one's means with all kinds of flavorful food and drink, as well as all necessary requisites offered within the great mandala, one should bestow this *siddhivajra* vow: "This is that very state of omniscience," and so forth.
Then, [the teacher] should declare the *śapathahṛdaya* (the heart-pledge) to all of them again, saying: "This must not be told to anyone."
Then, having sent forth those who have entered, having praised [the deity] again with the hundred-and-eight names,

having worshipped with the *lāsya* dance and other offerings, having prostrated and offered the *argha*, having dedicated the merit for the attainment of one's desired goal, having performed the release of the mudrā, and having bound the *sattvavajrī* mudrā—

Having circumambulated the maṇḍala three or seven times and performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) and other rites as before, one should dissolve the maṇḍala with the mantra beginning "The letter *A* is the mouth" (*akāro mukham*). One then casts the floral offerings (*nirmālya*) and other remains into water.
Then, having uprooted all the stakes with the four *huṃ* syllables, [one recites]:
*oṃ ruru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhane svāhā*.
Having recited this one hundred and eight times, one should bathe all the stakes and the natural ground with milk, and fill in the pits.

(86) Having prepared a ritual fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) for all rites facing the entrance door, one should perform a peaceful burnt offering (*śāntihoma*), focusing upon oneself, the disciples, the king, and all sentient beings.

Then, having positioned the principal disciple on his left side, he should duly offer one hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Vajrasattva mantra. Thereafter, he should perform eight hundred oblations with the Buddhalocanā mantra. Then, having bound that very mudrā...
One hundred oblations of jujube fruits, rice, and sesame seeds.

Then, having sprinkled water over his head that has been consecrated by the Vajrayakṣa mantra, one should tie a protective thread upon his left hand with that same [mantra]. Then, touching his heart with the hand, one should recite [the mantra] seven times.

For others here, one should offer the seven sets of seven oblations as previously described. Then, one should perform the sprinkling of water, the binding of the protection-thread, and the touching with the heart-mantra.
Whatever merit has been accumulated by me through the performance of the *Sarvavajrodaya*, which bestows all the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the beings such as Vajrasattva and others— (1).
The foremost of vidyās, whose womb is bliss, the sole kinsman of all sentient beings—by him the entire world is [pervaded]; he is the all-pervading Mahāvajradhara. (2)

The *Sarvavajrodaya*, titled "The Means for the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm," extracted from the *Śrīmad-Ārya-sarvatathāgata-tattvasaṃgraha*, the Great Mahāyāna Abhisamaya, the Great King of Tantras, is hereby completed.
This was composed by the venerable Mahāvajrācārya Ānandagarbha.
By whatever merit has been acquired by me through this writing, purified by my spiritual practice, may this entire world become the manifestation of Śrī Vajra.
It was written by Ratnākara, for the purpose of establishing all sentient beings without exception in supreme nirvāṇa. Saṃvat Acūte.
